function getParameterByName(name, url) {
		if(url == null){
		  url = window.location.href;
		}
	    name = name.replace(/[\[\]]/g, '\\$&');
	    var regex = new RegExp('[?&]' + name + '(=([^&#]*)|&|#|$)'),
		results = regex.exec(url);
	    if (!results) return null;
	    if (!results[2]) return '';
	    return decodeURIComponent(results[2].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
	}

<script type="application/ld+json">{"@context":"https:\/\/schema.org","@type":"BlogPosting","headline":"01flip: Multi-Platform Ransomware Written in Rust","name":"01flip: Multi-Platform Ransomware Written in Rust","description":"01flip is a new ransomware family fully written in Rust. Activity linked to 01flip points to alleged dark web data leaks. ","url":"https:\/\/unit42.paloaltonetworks.com\/new-ransomware-01flip-written-in-rust\/","mainEntityOfPage":"https:\/\/unit42.paloaltonetworks.com\/new-ransomware-01flip-written-in-rust\/","datePublished":"December 10, 2025","articleBody":"Executive Summary\r\nIn June 2025, we observed a new ransomware family named 01flip targeting a limited set of victims in the Asia-Pacific region. 01flip ransomware is fully written in the Rust programming language and supports multi-platform architectures by leveraging the cross-compilation feature of Rust.\r\n\r\nThese financially motivated attackers likely carried this out through manual means. We have confirmed an alleged data leak from an affected organization on a dark web forum shortly after the attack. We are currently tracking this activity as CL-CRI-1036, signifying a cluster of malicious activity that is likely related to cybercrime.\r\n\r\nOur key findings are:\r\n\r\n \tFinancially motivated attackers behind CL-CRI-1036 use 01flip ransomware, a newly observed ransomware family purely written in Rust\r\n \tThis ransomware supports multi-platform architecture, including Windows and Linux\r\n \tA threat actor potentially associated with CL-CRI-1036 is offering data for sale on dark web forums (likely stolen with 01flip ransomware)\r\n\r\nWhile the impact of CL-CRI-1036 is limited at this point, it\u2019s likely that this activity is related to alleged data leaks.\r\n\r\nPalo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats described through the following products and services:\r\n\r\n \tAdvanced WildFire\r\n \tCortex XDR and XSIAM\r\n \tCortex Xpanse\r\n\r\nIf you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nRelated Unit 42 Topics\r\nRust, Sliver, Ransomware, Cybercrime\r\n\r\n\r\n\r\nBackground\r\nIn early June 2025, Unit 42 researchers investigated a suspicious Windows executable. The executable caught our attention because it is a Rust-based binary that exhibited ransomware-like behavior in our sandbox.\r\n\r\nOur initial analysis revealed that this is a new ransomware family fully written in Rust, called \u201c01flip.\u201d This name is based on the appended file extension (.01flip) and the email address (01Flip@proton[.]me) found in the ransom note.\r\n\r\nAfter further investigation, we discovered a Linux version of 01flip ransomware, which showed zero detection rate at least three months after the sample had initially been submitted to VirusTotal.\r\nCampaign Overview\r\nVictimology\r\nAt the time of writing, we observed a minimal set of victims. But victims of this ransomware include organizations responsible for critical infrastructure in Southeast Asia.\r\n\r\nAfter further investigation, we found a post on an online security forum by an alleged victim of 01flip ransomware, claiming that attackers had compromised their Zimbra Server, which is an email solution for enterprises.\r\n\r\nDue to the lack of information about victims, we assume that the use of 01flip ransomware is at a very early stage. However, there might be several victims in the Philippines and Taiwan, based on a post in a dark web forum that we believe comes from a threat actor linked to CL-CRI-1036.\r\nInitial Access\r\nInvestigation revealed that attackers had been attempting exploits targeting older vulnerabilities such as CVE-2019-11580 against a victim\u2019s internet-facing applications since early April 2025. It is unclear which activities specifically succeeded in granting attackers access to this system. However, a month later, they successfully deployed a Linux version of Sliver, a publicly available cross-platform adversary emulation framework written in Go.\r\nPost-Exploitation\r\nIn late May 2025, the threat actor behind CL-CRI-1036 successfully performed lateral movement to another Linux machine by downloading another Sliver implant, which was a TCP Pivot profiled implant. A week later, we confirmed that attackers deployed multiple 01flip ransomware instances onto many devices within the network, including both Windows and Linux machines.\r\n\r\nThe exact methods the attackers used to deploy the ransomware after the initial compromise remain unclear. However, given the rapid distribution of the ransomware to multiple devices, it is highly likely that the attackers conducted the following activities, possibly through Sliver and its modules:\r\n\r\n \tHands-on reconnaissance\r\n \tCredential dumping\r\n \tLateral movement\r\n\r\nTechnical Analysis of 01flip Ransomware\r\nInitial Analysis\r\nAs of late October, we had observed both Windows and Linux versions of 01flip ransomware. The 01flip ransomware sample is not packed or heavily obfuscated, unlike other malware used by cybercriminals. Therefore, we can easily identify that it is compiled from Rust source code, due to the file extension (.rs), as shown in Figure 1.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167861\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 1. Visible Rust-related strings in the 01flip ransomware sample.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nFigure 2 shows the differences in results using rustbininfo between the Windows and Linux platform samples. The rustbininfo tool generates a list of dependencies (known as \u201ccrates\u201d in Rust), which we used to compare the two samples.\r\n\r\nAside from architecture-specific libraries, we can see that the Rust version, commit hash and library versions mostly match. Therefore, most of the functionality is identical, but we also noticed a few differences that we will describe later.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167872\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 2. The two 01flip ransomware samples used mostly the same crates (left: Windows, right: Linux).[\/caption]\r\n\r\nThe Rust compiler generally produces more complex assembly code than traditional C\/C++ compilers. This added complexity can make reverse engineering Rust malware challenging for malware analysts. Despite this, the malware\u2019s capabilities are simple and straightforward.\r\nRansomware Functionality\r\nThe following are key functions of 01flip ransomware:\r\n\r\n \tEnumerating all possible drives (e.g., from A: to Z:)\r\n \tCreating ransom notes, RECOVER-YOUR-FILE.TXT, in all writable directories\r\n \tRenaming files containing specific file extensions with the following naming convention: &lt;ORIGINAL_FILENAME&gt;.&lt;UNIQUE_ID&gt;.&lt;0 or 1&gt;.01flip\r\n \tEncrypting files using AES-128-CBC and RSA-2048\r\n \tDeleting itself\r\n\r\nDefense Evasion Techniques\r\n01flip ransomware employs several evasion techniques. For example, both Linux and Windows versions are designed to use low-level APIs or system calls as much as possible, because such activity is less likely to stand out from normal operating system activity. Figure 3 shows an example of native APIs used in our sample of the Windows version of 01flip ransomware.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167883\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 3. Example of low-level native APIs used to read\/write files in the Windows version.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nAdditionally, most of the user-defined strings in the ransomware code are encoded. These strings are decoded at runtime:\r\n\r\n \tThe ransom note content\r\n \tThe ransom note filename\r\n \tThe extension list\r\n \tThe RSA public key\r\n\r\nThe algorithm decodes each encoded string by performing a SUB operation every two bytes as follows.\r\nfrom more_itertools import chunked\r\n\r\ndef decrypt_string(enc: bytes) -&gt; str:\r\n\r\nreturn ''.join(chr(chunk[0] - chunk[1]) for chunk in chunked(enc, 2))\r\nEncoded strings are embedded in the .text or .data section of the Windows variant based on their length. Figure 4 demonstrates how 01flip ransomware decodes the ransom note template.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167894\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 4. How 01flip ransomware decodes the ransom note stored with its binary.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nTechniques like invoking system calls and encoded strings are not an effective evasion strategy on their own. Because the 01flip ransomware sample we analyzed works as designed in a sandbox environment, it is still relatively easy to detect.\r\n\r\nMost ransomware is relatively straightforward and noisy. However, some of the 01flip ransomware samples implement a simple anti-sandbox technique by checking whether the filename contains the string 01flip. If the sample's filename contains the string 01flip, the ransomware proceeds to indicator removal without performing file encryption.\r\nData Encryption\r\n01flip ransomware drops ransom notes in all writable directories before encrypting files. These ransom notes contain contact information and cipher data that is required to obtain a key to decrypt a victim's files, as shown in Figure 5.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167905\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 5. Example of a 01flip ransom note.[\/caption]\r\n\r\n01flip ransomware excludes files with specific extensions from encryption. This encryption exclusion extension list can be found in the Appendix. Finally, 01flip encrypts files using the AES encryption algorithm. The session key used for the ransomware's file-encrypting activity is itself encrypted using an embedded RSA public key. Figure 6 shows an example of this RSA key.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167916\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 6. RSA public key from the 01flip ransomware sample.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nEncrypted files are renamed with the specific naming convention &lt;ORIGINAL_FILENAME&gt;.&lt;UNIQUE_ID&gt;.&lt;0 or 1&gt;.01flip, as shown in Figure 7.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167927\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 7. Example of encrypted filenames in a Windows environment infected with 01flip ransomware.[\/caption]\r\nIndicator Removal\r\nAfter completing encryption, the 01flip ransomware attempts to remove any trace of itself, to prevent it from being recovered from an infected host. The Windows and Linux variants invoke the following commands, respectively, after replacing ${self_name} with its current filename.\r\n# Windows\r\n\r\nping 127.0.0.7 -n 5 &gt; Nul &amp; fsutil file setZeroData offset=0 length=4194303 ${self_name} &gt; Nul &amp; Del \/f \/q ${self_name}\r\n# Linux\r\n\r\nsleep 5 &amp;&amp; dd if=\/dev\/urandom of=${self_name} bs=1M count=4 &gt; \/dev\/null 2&gt;&amp;1 &amp;&amp; rm ${self_name} &gt; \/dev\/null 2&gt;&amp;1\r\nPossible Attribution\r\nAttacker Activity\r\nAttackers behind this campaign have so far demanded one bitcoin (BTC) for decrypting files. Communication with the attackers takes place in a secure email or in a private messaging channel. Figure 8 shows an example of the demand through messaging channel text.\r\n\r\nAs of late October, the attackers behind CL-CRI-1036 don't appear to operate a double extortion site like those commonly seen in recent ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) groups.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167938\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 8. Message from the attackers in a private messaging channel.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nFurther investigation revealed an alleged data leak of the affected organization on a dark web forum posted on the day after the ransomware deployment. Figure 9 shows this post. While we were unable to verify the legitimacy of the post, the data appears to be credible based on the positive reactions of other users in the forum.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167949\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"1000\"] Figure 9. Post of the alleged data leak on a dark web forum.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nWhile this user who made this post has been registered in this forum since April 2023, we were able to confirm only three posts since June 2025. The post indicates that victims in Taiwan and the Philippines were also targeted. The username itself is not particularly unique, but we have confirmed that a Russian-speaking user with the same username has been selling data and network access on the well-known dark web forum XSS since 2020.\r\n\r\nOf note, 01flip ransomware cannot exfiltrate data, so the only connection between this poster and 01flip is the victim.\r\nPossible Overlap With LockBit?\r\nDuring our analysis of 01flip ransomware, we found that there is one particularly interesting extension in the list of file extensions excluded from encryption, which is lockbit as shown in Figure 10.\r\n\r\n[caption id=\"attachment_167960\" align=\"alignnone\" width=\"600\"] Figure 10. Lockbit extension in the list of file extensions excluded from encryption by the 01flip ransomware sample.[\/caption]\r\n\r\nAvoiding encrypting files with a lockbit file extension implies a possible overlap of the threat actor behind CL-CRI-1036 and the group behind LockBit ransomware, which we track as Flighty Scorpius. However, other than this odd bit of code, we can find no other connection between these two ransomware families.\r\nConclusion\r\nWe have described emerging activity, which we currently track as CL-CRI-1036, where financially motivated attackers used a new Rust-based ransomware named 01flip. This activity highlights the challenges faced by defenders from attackers using modern programming languages in malware development. Based on our analysis, this campaign seems to be in its early stages and may be related to an alleged data leak on a dark web forum.\r\nPalo Alto Networks Protection and Mitigation\r\nPalo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products:\r\n\r\n \tTheAdvanced WildFire machine-learning models and analysis techniques have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.\r\n \tCortex XDR and XSIAM help prevent the threats outlined in this blog by employing the Malware Prevention Engine. This approach combines several layers of protection, including WildFire, Behavioral Threat Protection and the Local Analysis module, to prevent both known and unknown malware from causing harm to endpoints.\r\n\r\nIn addition, the Anti-Ransomware module enables Cortex XDR to protect against encryption-based activity associated with ransomware, to help analyze and halt ransomware before any data loss occurs.\r\n\r\n \tCortex Xpanse can help detect internet-facing instances of insecure software, such as Atlassian Crowd Server, which was noted as being exploited by CVE-2019-11580 and leading to initial access.\r\n\r\nCortex Xpanse has an Attack Surface Rule for \u201cInsecure Atlassian Crowd Server\u201d meant to identify this example, as well as many other detections out of the box for applications with RCE vulnerabilities which are attractive for Ransomware operators.\r\n\r\nAll detections in Cortex Xpanse are also available in Cortex XSIAM as part of the Attack Surface Management (ASM) add-on.\r\n\r\nIf you think you may have been compromised or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the Unit 42 Incident Response team or call:\r\n\r\n \tNorth America: Toll Free: +1 (866) 486-4842 (866.4.UNIT42)\r\n \tUK: +44.20.3743.3660\r\n \tEurope and Middle East: +31.20.299.3130\r\n \tAsia: +65.6983.8730\r\n \tJapan: +81.50.1790.0200\r\n \tAustralia: +61.2.4062.7950\r\n \tIndia: 000 800 050 45107\r\n \tSouth Korea: +82.080.467.8774\r\n\r\nPalo Alto Networks has shared these findings with our fellow Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) members. CTA members use this intelligence to rapidly deploy protections to their customers and to systematically disrupt malicious cyber actors. Learn more about the Cyber Threat Alliance.\r\nIndicators of Compromise\r\nMalicious Samples\r\nWindows Version of 01flip Ransomware\r\n\r\n \tSHA-256 hash: 6aad1c36ab9c7c44350ebe3a17178b4fd93c2aa296e2af212ab28d711c0889a3\r\n \tFile size: 741,888 bytes\r\n \tFile type: PE32+ executable (GUI) x86-64 (stripped to external PDB), for MS Windows\r\n\r\nLinux Version of 01flip Ransomware\r\n\r\n \tSHA-256 hash: e5834b7bdd70ec904470d541713e38fe933e96a4e49f80dbfb25148d9674f957\r\n \tFile size: 948,640 bytes\r\n \tFile type: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), static-pie linked, stripped\r\n\r\nLinux Sliver Beacon, TCP Pivot as C2\r\n\r\n \tSHA-256 hash: ba41f0c7ea36cefe7bc9827b3cf27308362a4d07a8c97109704df5d209bce191\r\n \tFile size: 13,414,400 bytes\r\n \tFile type: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped\r\n\r\nAppendix: Encryption Exclusion Extension List\r\nA-L\r\n\r\n \t01flip\r\n     ;(function(win, doc, style, timeout) {
    var STYLE_ID = 'at-body-style';
    function getParent() {
    return doc.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
    }
    function addStyle(parent, id, def) {
        if (!parent) {
        return;
        }
        var style = doc.createElement('style');
        style.id = id;
        style.innerHTML = def;
        parent.appendChild(style);
    }
    function removeStyle(parent, id) {
        if (!parent) {
            return;
        }
        var style = doc.getElementById(id);
        if (!style) {
            return;
        }
        parent.removeChild(style);
    }
    addStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID, style);
    setTimeout(function() {
    removeStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID);
    }, timeout);
    }(window, document, "body {visibility:hidden !important}", 3000));

    /**
 * String.prototype.replaceAll() polyfill
 * https://gomakethings.com/how-to-replace-a-section-of-a-string-with-another-one-with-vanilla-js/
 * @author Chris Ferdinandi
 * @license MIT
 */
if (!String.prototype.replaceAll) {
	String.prototype.replaceAll = function(str, newStr){
		// If a regex pattern
		if (Object.prototype.toString.call(str).toLowerCase() === '[object regexp]') {
			return this.replace(str, newStr);
		}
		// If a string
		return this.replace(new RegExp(str, 'g'), newStr);
	};
}

<script type="text/javascript">
	function getCookie(cname) {
	 	var name = cname + "=";
  		var decodedCookie = decodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
		var ca = decodedCookie.split(';');
  		for(var i = 0; i <ca.length; i++) {
    			var c = ca[i];
    			while (c.charAt(0) == ' ') {
     				 c = c.substring(1);
    			}
    			if (c.indexOf(name) == 0) {
    				 return c.substring(name.length, c.length);
    			}
  		}
  		return "";
	}

	var referer = "";//sessionStorage.container;
	var pcontainer = sessionStorage.getItem("container");
	var searchResultsPagePath = "";
	if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Prisma')!=-1)){
	    referer = 'Prisma' ;
	}        
        else if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Cortex')!=-1)){
            if( pcontainer.indexOf('CloudCortex') != -1){
                referer = 'CloudCortex' ;
            }
            else{
                referer = 'Cortex' ;
            }	    
	}
        else if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Sase')!=-1)){
	    referer = 'Sase' ;
	}
	else if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Unit')!=-1)){
	    referer = 'Unit' ;
	}
	else if(((pcontainer) && pcontainer.indexOf('Ngfw')!=-1)){
	    referer = 'Ngfw' ;
	}
        var fromRef = document.referrer;
        var nContainer = getCookie("navContainer");
        if(nContainer){//If user is coming from main site, we need to reset the container		
		if(fromRef  && fromRef.indexOf("prismacloud.io")!=-1){
                        referer = 'Prisma' ;
                        sessionStorage.setItem("container","Prisma");
                } else if(fromRef.indexOf("paloaltonetworks.com")!=-1 || fromRef.indexOf("paloaltonetworks.jp")!=-1 ){
                        if(nContainer.indexOf('Prisma') != -1){
                            referer = 'Prisma' ;
                            sessionStorage.setItem("container","Prisma");
                        }
                        if(nContainer.indexOf('Cortex') != -1){
                            if( nContainer.indexOf('CloudCortex') != -1){
                                referer = 'CloudCortex';
                                sessionStorage.setItem("container","CloudCortex");
                            }
                            else{
                                referer = 'Cortex';
                                sessionStorage.setItem("container","Cortex");
                            }                            
                        }
			if(nContainer.indexOf('Sase') != -1){
                            referer = 'Sase' ;
                            sessionStorage.setItem("container","Sase");
                        }
			if(nContainer.indexOf('Unit') != -1){
                            referer = 'Unit' ;
                            sessionStorage.setItem("container","Unit");
                        }
			if(nContainer.indexOf('Ngfw') != -1){
                            referer = 'Ngfw' ;
                            sessionStorage.setItem("container","Ngfw");
                        }
			document.cookie = 'navContainer=; path=/; domain=.paloaltonetworks.com; expires=' + new Date(0).toUTCString();
		}
	}
if(referer != "Prisma" && referer != "CloudCortex" && referer != "Cortex" && referer != "Sase" && referer != "Unit" && referer != "Ngfw") {
    referer = 'Unit' ;
    sessionStorage.setItem("container","Unit");
}
function callMainSitePrismaNavHTML(){
    
    var referrer_domain = 'https://www.paloaltonetworks.com';
    sessionStorage.setItem("domain",referrer_domain);
    if(referer == 'Prisma'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderPrisma.prismaRenderer.html';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=prisma&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/prismasearch";
        }
    if(referer == 'CloudCortex'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=cortexcloud&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexcloudsearch";	
    }
    if(referer == 'Cortex'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderCortex.cortexRenderer.html';	
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=cortex&domain=en';	
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexsearch";	
    }
    if(referer == 'Sase'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderSase.saseRenderer.html';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=sase&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/sasesearch";
    }
    if(referer == 'Unit'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=unit42&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/content/pan/en_US/search/unit42search";
		    }
    if(referer == 'Ngfw'){
        //var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/ngfw-cdss-nav-renderer.php';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=ngfw&domain=en'; 
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/ngfwcdsssearch";
    }
    httpGet(menu_url,'menu_html');
    document.getElementById('main-nav-menu-cont').removeAttribute("style");
}
function addStyle(styles) {            
    /* Create style document */
    var css = document.createElement('style');
    css.type = 'text/css';

    if (css.styleSheet) 
        css.styleSheet.cssText = styles;
    else 
        css.appendChild(document.createTextNode(styles));

    /* Append style to the tag name */
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(css);
}
function httpGet(theUrl,req_type) {
    if (window.XMLHttpRequest) { // code for IE7+, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari
        xmlhttp=new XMLHttpRequest();
    } else {// code for IE6, IE5
        xmlhttp=new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
    }
    xmlhttp.onreadystatechange=function()
    {
        if (xmlhttp.readyState==4 && xmlhttp.status==200)
        {
            if(req_type == 'menu_html'){
            var nav_text = xmlhttp.responseText.replaceAll('https://static.cloud.coveo.com/searchui/v2.9159/js/CoveoJsSearch.Lazy.min.js', '');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll('src="/', 'src="'+maindomain_lang+'/');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("'/content", "'"+maindomain_lang+"/content");
                        
            document.getElementById("PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC").innerHTML = nav_text.replaceAll('href="/', 'href="'+maindomain_lang+'/');

            var lozad_back = document.getElementsByClassName('lozad-background');
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(lozad_back, function(el) {
            // Do stuff here
            var el_back_img_path = el.getAttribute('data-background-image');
            var first_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'");
            var last_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'",first_pos+1);
            el_back_img_path = el_back_img_path.substring(first_pos+1,last_pos);
            el.setAttribute("data-background-image",main_site_url+el_back_img_path);
            });
            const observer_lozad = lozad('.lozad, .lozad-background'); // lazy loads elements with default selector as '.lozad'
            observer_lozad.observe();
            }
            if(req_type == 'head_inline_css'){
            addStyle(xmlhttp.responseText);
            }
        }
    }
    xmlhttp.open("GET", theUrl, true );
    xmlhttp.send();    
}    
    
if(referer == 'Prisma' || referer == 'CloudCortex' || referer == 'Cortex' || referer == 'Sase' || referer == 'Unit' || referer == 'Ngfw'){
    const article = document.querySelector('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC');
    if(referer == 'Prisma'){
        article.dataset.type = 'prisma';
        $('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC').removeClass('default').addClass('defaultRedesigned');
    }
    else if(referer == 'CloudCortex'){
        article.dataset.type = 'cloudcortex';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Cortex'){
        article.dataset.type = 'cortex';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Sase'){
        article.dataset.type = 'sase';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Unit'){
        article.dataset.type = 'unit';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Ngfw'){
        article.dataset.type = 'ngfw';
    }
    //set class to default
    if(referer == 'Unit' || referer == 'Ngfw'){
        $('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC').removeClass('default').addClass('defaultRedesigned');
    }
    callMainSitePrismaNavHTML();
}

    <section class="section blog-contents"> 
      <div class="pa blog-editor">

            <div class="be__contents">
              <div class="be__contents-wrapper">
                <h2><a id="post-167849-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>In June 2025, we observed a new ransomware family named 01flip targeting a limited set of victims in the Asia-Pacific region. 01flip ransomware is fully written in the Rust programming language and supports multi-platform architectures by leveraging the cross-compilation feature of Rust.</p>
<p>These financially motivated attackers likely carried this out through manual means. We have confirmed an alleged data leak from an affected organization on a dark web forum shortly after the attack. We are currently <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/unit-42-attribution-framework/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">tracking this activity</a> as CL-CRI-1036, signifying a cluster of malicious activity that is likely related to cybercrime.</p>
<p>Our key findings are:</p>
<ul>
<li>Financially motivated attackers behind CL-CRI-1036 use 01flip ransomware, a newly observed ransomware family purely written in Rust</li>
<li>This ransomware supports multi-platform architecture, including Windows and Linux</li>
<li>A threat actor potentially associated with CL-CRI-1036 is offering data for sale on dark web forums (likely stolen with 01flip ransomware)</li>
</ul>
<p>While the impact of CL-CRI-1036 is limited at this point, it’s likely that this activity is related to alleged data leaks.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats described through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a></li>
<li><a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XDR" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xsiam" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xpanse" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex Xpanse</a></li>
</ul>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">
<thead>
<tr>
<td style="width: 35%;"><b>Related Unit 42 Topics</b></td>
<td style="width: 100%;"><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tag/rust/" target="_blank" rel="noopener"><b>Rust</b></a>, <strong><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tag/sliver/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Sliver</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/category/ransomware/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Ransomware</a></strong>, <strong><a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/category/cybercrime/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cybercrime</a></strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
</table>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_kairq4qvu4b7"></a>Background</h2>
<p>In early June 2025, Unit 42 researchers investigated a suspicious Windows executable. The executable caught our attention because it is a Rust-based binary that exhibited ransomware-like behavior in our sandbox.</p>
<p><a href="https://github.com/PaloAltoNetworks/Unit42-timely-threat-intel/blob/main/2025-06-24-IOCs-for-01flip-ransomware.txt" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Our initial analysis</a> revealed that this is a new ransomware family fully written in Rust, called “01flip.” This name is based on the appended file extension (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.01flip)</span> and the email address (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">01Flip@proton[.]me</span>) found in the ransom note.</p>
<p>After further investigation, we discovered a <a href="https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/e5834b7bdd70ec904470d541713e38fe933e96a4e49f80dbfb25148d9674f957/details" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Linux version of 01flip ransomware</a>, which showed zero detection rate at least three months after the sample had initially been submitted to VirusTotal.</p>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_ea2k942oqsb0"></a>Campaign Overview</h2>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_dibdcphzoajk"></a>Victimology</h3>
<p>At the time of writing, we observed a minimal set of victims. But victims of this ransomware include organizations responsible for critical infrastructure in Southeast Asia.</p>
<p>After further investigation, we found <a href="https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/forums/t/808867/unknown-01flip-ext-ransomware-attack-zimbra-server/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">a post on an online security forum</a> by an alleged victim of 01flip ransomware, claiming that attackers had compromised their Zimbra Server, which is an email solution for enterprises.</p>
<p>Due to the lack of information about victims, we assume that the use of 01flip ransomware is at a very early stage. However, there might be several victims in the Philippines and Taiwan, based on a post in a dark web forum that we believe comes from a threat actor linked to CL-CRI-1036.</p>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_irg5yhf24r1s"></a>Initial Access</h3>
<p>Investigation revealed that attackers had been attempting exploits targeting older vulnerabilities such as <a href="https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2019-11580" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CVE-2019-11580</a> against a victim’s internet-facing applications since early April 2025. It is unclear which activities specifically succeeded in granting attackers access to this system. However, a month later, they successfully deployed a Linux version of <a href="https://github.com/BishopFox/sliver" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Sliver</a>, a publicly available cross-platform adversary emulation framework written in Go.</p>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_m5br7fmv7ver"></a>Post-Exploitation</h3>
<p>In late May 2025, the threat actor behind CL-CRI-1036 successfully performed lateral movement to another Linux machine by downloading another Sliver implant, which was a <a href="https://github.com/BishopFox/sliver/wiki/Pivots/d87b3e15111e7be50dd885be966c35bca629c626#tcp-pivots" target="_blank" rel="noopener">TCP Pivot</a> profiled implant. A week later, we confirmed that attackers deployed multiple 01flip ransomware instances onto many devices within the network, including both Windows and Linux machines.</p>
<p>The exact methods the attackers used to deploy the ransomware after the initial compromise remain unclear. However, given the rapid distribution of the ransomware to multiple devices, it is highly likely that the attackers conducted the following activities, possibly through Sliver and its modules:</p>
<ul>
<li>Hands-on reconnaissance</li>
<li>Credential dumping</li>
<li>Lateral movement</li>
</ul>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_wven14kmgum2"></a>Technical Analysis of 01flip Ransomware</h2>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_174p52qw2iub"></a>Initial Analysis</h3>
<p>As of late October, we had observed both Windows and Linux versions of 01flip ransomware. The 01flip ransomware sample is not packed or heavily obfuscated, unlike other malware used by cybercriminals. Therefore, we can easily identify that it is compiled from Rust source code, due to the file extension (<span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.rs</span>), as shown in Figure 1.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167861" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167861" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167861 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-95980-167849-1.png" alt="Screenshot of displaying a list of file paths in a code repository related to different program versions and components. The file name extensions are highlighted in yellow." width="1000" height="414" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-95980-167849-1.png 1388w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-95980-167849-1-786x325.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-95980-167849-1-768x318.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167861" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. Visible Rust-related strings in the 01flip ransomware sample.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Figure 2 shows the differences in results using <a href="https://github.com/N0fix/rustbininfo" target="_blank" rel="noopener">rustbininfo</a> between the Windows and Linux platform samples. The rustbininfo tool generates a list of dependencies (known as “crates” in Rust), which we used to compare the two samples.</p>
<p>Aside from architecture-specific libraries, we can see that the Rust version, commit hash and library versions mostly match. Therefore, most of the functionality is identical, but we also noticed a few differences that we will describe later.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167872" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167872" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167872 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2.png" alt="Two side-by-side screenshots of 01flip ransomware samples, mostly written in the Rust programming language. The left sample is Windows with certain lines highlighted in red and the right is Linux with certain lines highlighted in green. " width="1000" height="579" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2-760x440.png 760w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2-1210x700.png 1210w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2-768x444.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-99127-167849-2-1536x889.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167872" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. The two 01flip ransomware samples used mostly the same crates (left: Windows, right: Linux).</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Rust compiler generally produces more complex assembly code than traditional C/C++ compilers. This added complexity can make reverse engineering Rust malware challenging for malware analysts. Despite this, the malware’s capabilities are simple and straightforward.</p>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_p4kajqosxo7h"></a>Ransomware Functionality</h3>
<p>The following are key functions of 01flip ransomware:</p>
<ol>
<li>Enumerating all possible drives (e.g., from <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">A:</span> to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Z:</span>)</li>
<li>Creating ransom notes, <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">RECOVER-YOUR-FILE.TXT</span>, in all writable directories</li>
<li>Renaming files containing specific file extensions with the following naming convention: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">&lt;ORIGINAL_FILENAME&gt;.&lt;UNIQUE_ID&gt;.&lt;0 or 1&gt;.01flip</span></li>
<li>Encrypting files using AES-128-CBC and RSA-2048</li>
<li>Deleting itself</li>
</ol>
<h4><a id="post-167849-_23n20zwjuqvs"></a>Defense Evasion Techniques</h4>
<p>01flip ransomware employs several evasion techniques. For example, both Linux and Windows versions are designed to use low-level APIs or system calls as much as possible, because such activity is less likely to stand out from normal operating system activity. Figure 3 shows an example of native APIs used in our sample of the Windows version of 01flip ransomware.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167883" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167883" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167883 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-105425-167849-3.png" alt="Screenshot showing two rows of data." width="1000" height="82" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-105425-167849-3.png 1366w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-105425-167849-3-786x64.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-105425-167849-3-768x63.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167883" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. Example of low-level native APIs used to read/write files in the Windows version.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Additionally, most of the user-defined strings in the ransomware code are encoded. These strings are decoded at runtime:</p>
<ul>
<li>The ransom note content</li>
<li>The ransom note filename</li>
<li>The extension list</li>
<li>The RSA public key</li>
</ul>
<p>The algorithm decodes each encoded string by performing a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">SUB</span> operation every two bytes as follows.</p><!-- Crayon Syntax Highlighter v_2.7.2_beta -->

		<div id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988" class="crayon-syntax crayon-theme-classic crayon-font-monaco crayon-os-pc print-yes notranslate" data-settings=" minimize scroll-mouseover wrap" style=" margin-top: 12px; margin-bottom: 12px; font-size: 12px !important; line-height: 15px !important;">
		
			<div class="crayon-toolbar" data-settings=" mouseover overlay hide delay" style="font-size: 12px !important;height: 18px !important; line-height: 18px !important;"><span class="crayon-title"></span>
			<div class="crayon-tools" style="font-size: 12px !important;height: 18px !important; line-height: 18px !important;"><div class="crayon-button crayon-nums-button" title="Toggle Line Numbers"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div><div class="crayon-button crayon-plain-button" title="Toggle Plain Code"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div><div class="crayon-button crayon-wrap-button" title="Toggle Line Wrap"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div><div class="crayon-button crayon-expand-button" title="Expand Code"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div><div class="crayon-button crayon-copy-button" title="Copy"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div><div class="crayon-button crayon-popup-button" title="Open Code In New Window"><div class="crayon-button-icon"></div></div></div></div>
			<div class="crayon-info" style="min-height: 16.8px !important; line-height: 16.8px !important;"></div>
			<div class="crayon-plain-wrap"><textarea  class="crayon-plain print-no" data-settings="dblclick" readonly style="-moz-tab-size:4; -o-tab-size:4; -webkit-tab-size:4; tab-size:4; font-size: 12px !important; line-height: 15px !important;">
from more_itertools import chunked

def decrypt_string(enc: bytes) -&gt; str:

return ''.join(chr(chunk[0] - chunk[1]) for chunk in chunked(enc, 2))</textarea></div>
			<div class="crayon-main" style="">
				<table class="crayon-table">
					<tr class="crayon-row">
				<td class="crayon-nums " data-settings="show">
					<div class="crayon-nums-content" style="font-size: 12px !important; line-height: 15px !important;"><div class="crayon-num" data-line="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-1">1</div><div class="crayon-num crayon-striped-num" data-line="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-2">2</div><div class="crayon-num" data-line="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-3">3</div><div class="crayon-num crayon-striped-num" data-line="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-4">4</div><div class="crayon-num" data-line="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-5">5</div></div>
				</td>
						<td class="crayon-code"><div class="crayon-pre" style="font-size: 12px !important; line-height: 15px !important; -moz-tab-size:4; -o-tab-size:4; -webkit-tab-size:4; tab-size:4;"><div class="crayon-line" id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-1"><span class="crayon-e">from </span><span class="crayon-e">more_itertools </span><span class="crayon-e">import </span><span class="crayon-e">chunked</span></div><div class="crayon-line crayon-striped-line" id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-2">&nbsp;</div><div class="crayon-line" id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-3"><span class="crayon-e">def </span><span class="crayon-e">decrypt_string</span><span class="crayon-sy">(</span><span class="crayon-i">enc</span><span class="crayon-sy">:</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-i">bytes</span><span class="crayon-sy">)</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span>-<span class="crayon-h">&gt;</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-i">str</span><span class="crayon-sy">:</span></div><div class="crayon-line crayon-striped-line" id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-4">&nbsp;</div><div class="crayon-line" id="crayon-693cab2047692218699988-5"><span class="crayon-st">return</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-s">''</span><span class="crayon-sy">.</span><span class="crayon-e">join</span><span class="crayon-sy">(</span><span class="crayon-e">chr</span><span class="crayon-sy">(</span><span class="crayon-i">chunk</span><span class="crayon-sy">[</span><span class="crayon-cn">0</span><span class="crayon-sy">]</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span>-<span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-i">chunk</span><span class="crayon-sy">[</span><span class="crayon-cn">1</span><span class="crayon-sy">]</span><span class="crayon-sy">)</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-st">for</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-e">chunk </span><span class="crayon-st">in</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-e">chunked</span><span class="crayon-sy">(</span><span class="crayon-i">enc</span><span class="crayon-sy">,</span><span class="crayon-h"> </span><span class="crayon-cn">2</span><span class="crayon-sy">)</span><span class="crayon-sy">)</span></div></div></td>
					</tr>
				</table>
			</div>
		</div>
<!-- [Format Time: 0.0002 seconds] -->
<p>Encoded strings are embedded in the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.text</span> or <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">.data</span> section of the Windows variant based on their length. Figure 4 demonstrates how 01flip ransomware decodes the ransom note template.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167894" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167894" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167894 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-107996-167849-4.png" alt="Screenshot of a computer screen displaying a ransomware note in a command line interface, with an email address provided for contact. Above the note is a block of binary. " width="1000" height="556" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-107996-167849-4.png 1348w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-107996-167849-4-786x437.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-107996-167849-4-1258x700.png 1258w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-107996-167849-4-768x427.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167894" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. How 01flip ransomware decodes the ransom note stored with its binary.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Techniques like invoking system calls and encoded strings are not an effective evasion strategy on their own. Because the 01flip ransomware sample we analyzed works as designed in a sandbox environment, it is still relatively easy to detect.</p>
<p>Most ransomware is relatively straightforward and noisy. However, some of the 01flip ransomware samples implement a simple anti-sandbox technique by checking whether the filename contains the string <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">01flip</span>. If the sample's filename contains the string <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">01flip</span>, the ransomware proceeds to <a href="https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1070/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">indicator removal</a> without performing file encryption.</p>
<h4><a id="post-167849-_ub4y0sqbt3pz"></a>Data Encryption</h4>
<p>01flip ransomware drops ransom notes in all writable directories before encrypting files. These ransom notes contain contact information and cipher data that is required to obtain a key to decrypt a victim's files, as shown in Figure 5.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167905" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167905" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167905 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-111270-167849-5.png" alt="A computer screen displaying a ransomware note titled &quot;RECOVER-YOUR-FILES.TXT&quot; in a text editing software. The note includes instructions not to restart the computer, an email contact &quot;mp@proton.me&quot; for decryption key, and a session address for further communication. Some information is redacted for security concerns. " width="1000" height="340" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-111270-167849-5.png 1894w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-111270-167849-5-786x267.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-111270-167849-5-768x261.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-111270-167849-5-1536x522.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167905" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. Example of a 01flip ransom note.</figcaption></figure>
<p>01flip ransomware excludes files with specific extensions from encryption. This encryption exclusion extension list can be found in the <a href="#post-167849-_570cbe1pdhwx">Appendix</a>. Finally, 01flip encrypts files using the AES encryption algorithm. The session key used for the ransomware's file-encrypting activity is itself encrypted using an embedded RSA public key. Figure 6 shows an example of this RSA key.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167916" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167916" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167916 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-114513-167849-6.png" alt="Image displaying a segment of cryptographic text with a blue background, specifically showing a public key starting with 'BEGIN PUBLIC KEY' and ending with 'END PUBLIC KEY'." width="1000" height="238" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-114513-167849-6.png 1292w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-114513-167849-6-786x187.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-114513-167849-6-768x183.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167916" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. RSA public key from the 01flip ransomware sample.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Encrypted files are renamed with the specific naming convention <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">&lt;ORIGINAL_FILENAME&gt;.&lt;UNIQUE_ID&gt;.&lt;0 or 1&gt;.01flip</span>, as shown in Figure 7.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167927" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167927" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167927 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-118024-167849-7.png" alt="Screenshot of a computer file explorer window showing three files: an image file named; a text file titled &quot;RECOVER-YOUR-FILE.TXT&quot;; and another image file." width="1000" height="238" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-118024-167849-7.png 1050w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-118024-167849-7-786x187.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-118024-167849-7-768x183.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167927" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. Example of encrypted filenames in a Windows environment infected with 01flip ransomware.</figcaption></figure>
<h4><a id="post-167849-_1d11raeagzfg"></a>Indicator Removal</h4>
<p>After completing encryption, the 01flip ransomware attempts to remove any trace of itself, to prevent it from being recovered from an infected host. The Windows and Linux variants invoke the following commands, respectively, after replacing <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">${self_name}</span> with its current filename.</p><!-- Crayon Syntax Highlighter v_2.7.2_beta -->

<p></p>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_3gjs5orya9ag"></a>Possible Attribution</h2>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_fizkhgvoeqwm"></a>Attacker Activity</h3>
<p>Attackers behind this campaign have so far demanded one bitcoin (BTC) for decrypting files. Communication with the attackers takes place in a secure email or in a private messaging channel. Figure 8 shows an example of the demand through messaging channel text.</p>
<p>As of late October, the attackers behind CL-CRI-1036 don't appear to operate a double extortion site like those commonly seen in recent ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) groups.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167938" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167938" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167938 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8.png" alt="Text requesting a transfer of 1 Bitcoin to a blurred-out address on a dark background." width="1000" height="228" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8-786x179.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8-1920x437.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8-768x175.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-120659-167849-8-1536x350.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167938" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 8. Message from the attackers in a private messaging channel.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Further investigation revealed an alleged data leak of the affected organization on a dark web forum posted on the day after the ransomware deployment. Figure 9 shows this post. While we were unable to verify the legitimacy of the post, the data appears to be credible based on the positive reactions of other users in the forum.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167949" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167949" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167949 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9.png" alt="Screenshot of a dark web forum with some of the title of a post and identifying information of the poster redacted or blurred. The screenshot refers to data leaks. " width="1000" height="330" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9-786x259.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9-1920x633.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9-768x253.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-123683-167849-9-1536x506.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167949" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 9. Post of the alleged data leak on a dark web forum.</figcaption></figure>
<p>While this user who made this post has been registered in this forum since April 2023, we were able to confirm only three posts since June 2025. The post indicates that victims in Taiwan and the Philippines were also targeted. The username itself is not particularly unique, but we have confirmed that a Russian-speaking user with the same username has been selling data and network access on the well-known dark web forum XSS since 2020.</p>
<p>Of note, 01flip ransomware cannot exfiltrate data, so the only connection between this poster and 01flip is the victim.</p>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_a0uxd765cfwu"></a>Possible Overlap With LockBit?</h3>
<p>During our analysis of 01flip ransomware, we found that there is one particularly interesting extension in the list of file extensions excluded from encryption, which is <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">lockbit</span> as shown in Figure 10.</p>
<figure id="attachment_167960" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-167960" style="width: 600px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-167960 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-126995-167849-10.png" alt="A screenshot of assembly code, showing various data declarations and comments on an IDE with blue background." width="600" height="750" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-126995-167849-10.png 816w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-126995-167849-10-352x440.png 352w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-126995-167849-10-560x700.png 560w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/word-image-126995-167849-10-768x960.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-167960" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 10. <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Lockbit</span> extension in the list of file extensions excluded from encryption by the 01flip ransomware sample.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Avoiding encrypting files with a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">lockbit</span> file extension implies a possible overlap of the threat actor behind CL-CRI-1036 and the group behind LockBit ransomware, which we track as Flighty Scorpius. However, other than this odd bit of code, we can find no other connection between these two ransomware families.</p>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_2an8ryq91inv"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>We have described emerging activity, which we currently track as CL-CRI-1036, where financially motivated attackers used a new Rust-based ransomware named 01flip. This activity highlights the challenges faced by defenders from attackers using modern programming languages in malware development. Based on our analysis, this campaign seems to be in its early stages and may be related to an alleged data leak on a dark web forum.</p>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_htthnu6ayyia"></a>Palo Alto Networks Protection and Mitigation</h3>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products:</p>
<ul>
<li>The<a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Advanced WildFire</a> machine-learning models and analysis techniques have been reviewed and updated in light of the indicators shared in this research.</li>
<li><a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/p/XDR">Cortex XDR</a> and <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xsiam" target="_blank" rel="noopener">XSIAM</a> help prevent the threats outlined in this blog by employing the <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XDR/Cortex-XDR-4.x-Documentation/Malware-protection" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Malware Prevention Engine</a>. This approach combines several layers of protection, including <a href="https://docs.paloaltonetworks.com/wildfire" target="_blank" rel="noopener">WildFire</a>, Behavioral Threat Protection and the Local Analysis module, to prevent both known and unknown malware from causing harm to endpoints.</li>
</ul>
<p>In addition, the <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XDR/Cortex-XDR-3.x-Documentation/Endpoint-protection-capabilities" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Anti-Ransomware module</a> enables Cortex XDR to protect against encryption-based activity associated with ransomware, to help analyze and halt ransomware before any data loss occurs.</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cortex-xpanse" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex Xpanse</a> can help detect internet-facing instances of insecure software, such as Atlassian Crowd Server, which was noted as being exploited by CVE-2019-11580 and leading to initial access.</li>
</ul>
<p>Cortex Xpanse has an <a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XPANSE/2/Cortex-Xpanse-Expander-User-Guide/Attack-surface-rules" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Attack Surface Rule</a> for “Insecure Atlassian Crowd Server” meant to identify this example, as well as many other detections out of the box for applications with RCE vulnerabilities which are attractive for Ransomware operators.</p>
<p>All detections in Cortex Xpanse are also available in Cortex XSIAM as part of the Attack Surface Management (ASM) add-on.</p>
<p>If you think you may have been compromised or have an urgent matter, get in touch with the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a> or call:</p>
<ul>
<li>North America: Toll Free: +1 (866) 486-4842 (866.4.UNIT42)</li>
<li>UK: +44.20.3743.3660</li>
<li>Europe and Middle East: +31.20.299.3130</li>
<li>Asia: +65.6983.8730</li>
<li>Japan: +81.50.1790.0200</li>
<li>Australia: +61.2.4062.7950</li>
<li>India: 000 800 050 45107</li>
<li>South Korea: +82.080.467.8774</li>
</ul>
<p>Palo Alto Networks has shared these findings with our fellow Cyber Threat Alliance (CTA) members. CTA members use this intelligence to rapidly deploy protections to their customers and to systematically disrupt malicious cyber actors. Learn more about the <a href="https://www.cyberthreatalliance.org" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cyber Threat Alliance</a>.</p>
<h2><a id="post-167849-_np1dg1galw0y"></a>Indicators of Compromise</h2>
<h3><a id="post-167849-_mmebfdovmbm"></a>Malicious Samples</h3>
<h4>Windows Version of 01flip Ransomware</h4>
<ul>
<li>SHA-256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">6aad1c36ab9c7c44350ebe3a17178b4fd93c2aa296e2af212ab28d711c0889a3</span></li>
<li>File size: 741,888 bytes</li>
<li>File type: PE32+ executable (GUI) x86-64 (stripped to external PDB), for MS Windows</li>
</ul>
<h4>Linux Version of 01flip Ransomware</h4>
<ul>
<li>SHA-256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">e5834b7bdd70ec904470d541713e38fe933e96a4e49f80dbfb25148d9674f957</span></li>
<li>File size: 948,640 bytes</li>
<li>File type: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), static-pie linked, stripped</li>
</ul>
<h4>Linux Sliver Beacon, TCP Pivot as C2</h4>
<ul>
<li>SHA-256 hash: <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">ba41f0c7ea36cefe7bc9827b3cf27308362a4d07a8c97109704df5d209bce191</span></li>
<li>File size: 13,414,400 bytes</li>
<li>File type: ELF 64-bit LSB executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped</li>
</ul>

                <div class="g-recaptcha" data-expired-callback="captchaExpires" data-callback="captchaComplete" data-sitekey="6Lc5EhgTAAAAAJa-DzE7EeWABasWg4LKv-R3ao6o"></div>

<script>

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
	window.captchaComplete = function() {
		subscribeSuccess = true;
		if ($(mail).val() != '' && isEmail($(mail).val())) {
			$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
		}
		setTimeout(function() {
			$(email).focus();
			$('.g-recaptcha iframe').attr('tabindex', '-1');
		}, 100)
	}
	window.captchaExpires = function() {
		subscribeSuccess = false;
		$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
	} 
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		if (!subscribeSuccess) {
			$('.error-recaptcha').removeClass('d-none');
		} else {
			$('.error-recaptcha').addClass('d-none');
		}

		if (success && subscribeSuccess) {
			$.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: form.serialize(),
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
		}
		return false;
	});
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	var captcha_loaded = false;
         if(!captcha_loaded){
            // recaptcha on foucs call
            $(document).on('change paste keyup', '#newsletter-email', function () {
               if($('.g-recaptcha').hasClass('d-none')){
                $('.g-recaptcha').removeClass('d-none');
               }
               if(!captcha_loaded ){
                  captcha_loaded  = true;
                  // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
                  var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                  var script = document.createElement('script');
                  script.type = 'text/javascript';
                  script.src = 'https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api.js?hl=en_US';
                  head.appendChild(script);
               }
            });
        }
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});
</script>

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}

}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};
